options.author: first read (Wonder)
options.case:
- keep Nekohachi's patter as work, not local colour His banter on the tram in p2-p10 is not decoration before the serious part begins; it is the act itself, carried on in public because passengers have become an audience and a comeback is professionally compulsory. Again at the meeting he tests jokes, misapplies the borrowed word "situation" (p67-p69), apologises, recovers, and feels the flatness when は、は、は does not come (p63). If English tidies this into witty repartee it ennobles him; if it renders it as broad dialect comedy it does to him exactly what his audiences do. For the English: he must never become quaint Cockney or stage-Japanese. Use dropped, run-on, self-interrupting colloquial syntax, repetitions and verbal tics in place of the sentence-ending な and the self-deprecating でげす forms, and let the dignity show through competence and generosity, not through making his grammar more respectable.
- keep the ramble, because the ramble is the consciousness The narration stays glued to Nekohachi's mind, and that mind does not proceed: on the tram it slides from a heckle to why a comedian must not laugh, to protecting a voice he does not drink for, to caterpillars in a ditch and cutworms that, like thieves and like himself, work only at night (p10-p14). The garden returns at every pressure point (p20, p31-p33, p100, p158, p172-p173) and is still what he offers the departing gentlemen at his own gate (p182). A fluent version that breaks this into themed paragraphs, or clarifies the transitions, has rationalised away the man. For the English: do not iron out the long, associative sentences in which cabbages, a bath, a fee and a son succeed one another, and do not cut the lists. Keep the repetitions - animals, vegetables, children, money - as repetitions: they are Berman's networks, the web the story is made of, not redundancy to be varied away.
- let 'The Tiger' stay a clumsy paraphrase, not a set piece Half the story is a second-hand retelling of Kume's tale of a comic actor cast as a tiger whose child finds him weeping in the wings (p48-p90). It would be easy to polish this into a moving story-within-the-story. In the text it arrives as reported talk, interrupted, jargon-dusted (シチュエイション, バック), and judged thin by everyone present. Its power for Nekohachi is precisely that this mediocre fiction has got his life: four sons, a gifted twelve-year-old he has moved to the suburbs to keep away from the yose (p50, p93-p95). Prettify the paraphrase and his response looks disproportionate; sentimentalise his response and the literati's cool verdict loses its sting. For the English: keep the embedded summary flat and a little long-winded, keep its pathos unlyrical, and keep Nekohachi's interventions in his own terms (a father should not let the child see it) rather than translating them into the group's critical vocabulary. Let the reader feel the identification before Nekohachi names 悲哀 for himself.
options.tradeoff: Protects Nekohachi's associative consciousness and professional patter, at the risk of under-stating the structural clash with the literati and the ending's undecidability.

options.author: crux check (Wonder)
options.case:
- The collision of languages is the action: close third-person narration saturated with Nekohachi's Edokko yose patter (でげす, な, self-deprecating jokes, internal 洒落 he performs even to himself) set against the literati's imported jargon (シチュエイション, バック, 現実主義/具体) that he literally cannot parse. He is never off stage—he swallows '小奈良の小大仏' (p8), turns a tram ride into a 高座 (p5-9), negotiates every humiliation as a gag—while they study that very compulsion as '悲哀' in Kume's '虎'. Strip the register gap and the plot (a mimic taken to a research society) has no tension left: his mishearings of 'situation' as a predicament he is trapped in (p53), his gratitude at being quoted back as criticism (p79-82), and his final triumph in performance (p124-136) all only register because we hear him thinking and speaking in a different tongue from theirs. For the English: Keep two audible Englishes unblended: Nekohachi in a working, comic, self-interrupting stage patter full of swallowed retorts and asides, the writers in flat, borrowed critical abstraction; never polish either into the same literary fluency, and let the reader feel when neither fully understands the other.
- The mirrored tiger must stay unresolved: Nekohachi condemns Fukai for letting his child see the debasing role (p91-95) and has moved to the suburbs to hide his own, yet eagerly performs, fishes for praise and a fee (p171-177), and misreads Kume's anonymous self-denunciation as proof Kume is a wit after his own heart (p103-110). The text itself flags that even his grief-stricken face is partly exaggeration he half-knows about (p91), and ends not in renunciation—he plans to retell the novel to his wife (p188)—but in a 'rare' humble, human feeling (p185) alongside gas-lamp advertising and the night's two coins. If the translation settles him as either dignified artist-victim (the literati's '悲哀' made true) or comic butt the reader pities from above, it picks the side the story refuses: his sorrow is real and performed at once, his pride in hiding the act from his sons coexists with delight that '例の猫八' is known (p37-39), and that undecidability is what the whole mirrored structure was built to produce. For the English: Hold the double exposure in the English: render his self-recognitions and the closing humility straight, without irony markers, ennoblement, or a softened/resolved ending, so the reader—not the prose—decides how much is insight and how much is act.
options.tradeoff: Protects the register collision and the unresolved sorrow/performance double exposure, at the risk of under-stating the ramble and repetitious networks as the substance of Nekohachi's consciousness.

fork.question: Do the two readings name the same crux in different words, or different cruxes — Nekohachi's associative performed consciousness as the form to preserve, versus the unblended collision of his tongue with the literati's and the unresolved tiger-mirror as the structure to preserve? They share patter and 'The Tiger', but each makes central what the other leaves secondary, and adopting one will direct choices the other would direct differently, so the text does not settle it as mere rewording.

data.reason: They name different things, not the same thing in different words: Option 0 makes the crux the preservation of Nekohachi's rambling, repetitious, professionally performed consciousness and the deliberate flatness of the embedded paraphrase, while Option 1 makes it the unblended clash of his English with the literati's and the refusal to resolve sorrow against performance. Because that difference will recur in register, paragraphing, the retelling and the ending, and being wrong about which governs would be expensive, this goes up as a fork.
data.say: Fork opened: the two readings name different cruxes — Option 0 centres Nekohachi's rambling performed consciousness and the flat embedded 'Tiger', Option 1 centres the unblended register collision and the unresolved tiger-mirror — so I recommend proceeding provisionally on Option 0, whose formal risks (rationalising the ramble, varying the repetitions, prettifying the paraphrase) are the least recoverable if lost in draft, until the editor rules. House log: Fork sent up on whether the crux is Nekohachi's associative patter-consciousness or the register collision and unresolved tiger-mirror, proceeding on the former pending the editor's ruling.
